author: Hannibal
text_post: I would try to do a posterior chain exercise, houston. I don't know how much weight you have (I'm only guessing because you seem to pull all the weight you have up to your face), but I recommend the kettlebell swing. If there was a suitable replacement for squats and deadlifts, it would probably be pistols for reps, sprints, and swings. The swing is sort of like a ballistic deadlift. You're not going to get bodybuilder jacked or anything, but at least you won't be neglecting your lower body.  One bonus is that you'll pound pussy like a jackhammer if you do a lot of swings.  Don't want to buy a 90 dollar piece of nonadjustable cast iron? Here's the solution. http://rosstraining.com/blog/2008/12/31/...nstration/ This shows you how to make a T handle so that you don't need to buy a bunch of kettlebells.  In all seriousness, anything you can do with a kettlebell, you can do with other equipment that is not only adjustable, but cheaper. People who claim that kettlebells are a magical form of training equipment are deluded, it's all Dragon Door marketing to the fitness hipster who reads more than he trains. edit: As far as a workout program is concerned There's one out there called "Program Minimum" from Enter the Kettlebell, where you do a program of swings and turkish getups and it's designed by Pavel Tsatsouline. He claims that, once you go heavy enough, you literally don't need any other exercise. He's also the same guy who said that the deadlift is the best posterior chain exercise and that the squat isn't entirely necessary if you're deadlifting heavy enough, so take that with a grain of salt.  Pavel's a big fan of abbreviated forms of training where you do a posterior chain exercise and an upper body pressing movement and you just work the fuck out of them. It definitely delivers, I did a deadlift/shoulder press program and I put forty pounds on my press and a hundred on the deadlift over a period of 6 weeks. If you want to do a lower body exercise with the weight you do have, I'd do the swing at least two days a week, if not three. Try to keep the weight somewhat heavy, start at 50-70 lbs and keep going up. Watch some youtube videos to figure out the form. Throw in some pistol squats to give your quads something to do. You can lower the weight on the swing and do them for timed intervals if you're not all about strength.  Then I'd probably alternate presses on different days, bench on one and standing shoulder press on another.  Throw in some pullups for good measure, or you can do pendlay rows.

author: Hannibal
text_post: I'd just keep the reps low, don't go to failure, and do many sets. If you can only do 3 pullups, then do one or two for something like 10 sets.  Use a cadence you're comfortable with, just don't use momentum to throw the weight around if you're training for maximal strength. I usually do something like 2 seconds up, 1 second pause, 2 seconds down.  When it comes to bodyweight stuff, you have to get strong before you get all that big. Bodyweight exercises aren't the best for massive amounts of hypertrophy, but it's free and you can do it anywhere.  My question is, how much do you weigh and about how tall are you and what sort of budget do you have for working out (this includes diet and amount of time)? As far as legs are concerned, I recommend doing regular bodyweight squats until you can do one legged squats. Once you can do one legged squats, do them until you're comfortable and then do explosive one legged squats for lowish reps and never to failure. You won't have the strongest legs ever, but they'll be pretty strong pound for pound.  Convict conditioning has a shitty squat progression. Here's a better one. 1)Bodyweight squats until you're comfortable 2)Lower yourself down on one leg and then go back up with two 3)Lower yourself down on one leg while holding onto  something (I like to use a door), then go back up with some assistance. 4)Gradually work up to where you don't need the door.  5)One legged jumps for height 6)One legged jumps for height and distance Introduce this shit gradually. I went from bodyweight squats to one legged squats over the course of about four months. Most of it isn't strength, but balance and flexibility.  Don't bother with that little stuff like side raises and hammer curls if you're a beginner. Stick to compound movements. Try to workout at least three days a week. Keep the reps somewhat low (except for legs, they need higher reps), do many sets, and stick to the basics. I like to pick two exercises and bust my ass on them for an hour.  As far as bodyweight is concerned, that would be Pullups Bodyweight squats Handstand work (if you can't do a handstand yet, work on your pushups until you can) Pushups So you could structure your workouts like this Squats Pushups Day 2 Handstand work Pullups So a sample routine would look like this, for example Monday Bodyweight squats 20 rep warmup Pistol squats 4 reps 6 sets each leg Pushups 10 rep regular pushup warmup Diamond pushups 5 reps 7 sets Wednesday Handstands for time 30 second "reps", 4 sets Pullups 3 reps 6 sets Any workout routine done with enthusiasm will make gains. One of my buddies busts out as many pushups and pullups as he can every morning and he goes for a sprint a couple times a week. He's been doing that for the last two and a half years and, although his physique isn't bodybuilder impressive, he's got at least twenty pounds on his identical brother. He may not be using the most efficient workout, but he likes what he does and he sticks with it. I have far more respect for his third world workout and his dedication to it than 90% of the people who show up to the gym on January 1st.  In other words, don't get too caught up in rep schemes. If you bust your ass, you will make gains. If you keep the reps low with a good amount of sets, you won't develop as much hypertrophy but you will build strength (you want to have a good strength/mass ratio for bodyweight exercises so that you can do the harder variations of each exercise, like one armed pushups). I would also do sprints if you're on a tight budget for equipment. Sprints can build some muscle on your legs and they make you more explosive all around. Don't fear the overtraining fairy. Provided you eat enough and sleep enough, you could work out twice a day if you felt like it. I recommend Monday/Tuesday/Thursday/Friday.

author: Hannibal
text_post: Pullups are one of those exercises where the easiest way to get better at them is to do many sets of them short of failure so that you get more efficient at the movement. If you want to know how much time to take between sets, most people say you should stay between 90 and 30 seconds between sets. I just say, take as much time as you need between sets to be able to do another one. Don't get too mechanical with this, working out should be fun, or at least a bit meditative.  Tim Ferriss is concerned with the prevalent 80/20 rule, where he thinks that if he does 20% of the effort, he'll get 80% of the results.  As far as bodyweight exercises are concerned, there is no suitable replacement for the squat or deadlift (which would be in that 20% effort = 80% of the gains margin). That, and there's no real way to incrementally add weight, so the next best thing is to increase volume with proficiency in the exercise. I prefer to add sets before adding reps. Do whatever you want with your rep/set scheme, but I'll give you some justification for why I do what I do.  One set to failure is better than no sets and is more time efficient than many sets to near failure (like two to three reps short of failure). I recommend doing many sets to near failure for a couple reasons 1) You're not going to be sore as shit all the time 2) You'll have more motivation to work out because you won't be sore as shit all the time 3) Many sets to near failure is easier to recover from. Quicker recovery is better because you will, in all probability, gain more than the Ferriss method of one set to failure. 4) Your body is smart, and one of the quickest ways to get stronger is to increase the efficiency of a movement. If you practice many sets to near failure, you increase the efficiency of the neural pathways that you use to complete the movement because, not only do you practice the movement more, you always use good form. Perfect practice makes perfect, that's the underlying concept of Hebbian Theory.  5) I'd like to think that it's better for your joints to be using proper form all the time. At the very least, using proper form by never going to failure reduces stupid injuries. If you're more interested in "bodybuilding" with bodyweight exercises, than just do somewhat massive amounts of pullups and pushups. There's no secret and there's no shortcut. You can say this guy has good genetics and you'd probably be right, but this guy right here is somewhere around 40 years old and, for the most part, he doesn't even use weights. He's got a better physique than most chair jockeys half his age who spend their time arguing about how much glutamine and shit to take after workouts. Al Kavadlo doesn't bother with that shit. He just eats clean, gets his shit done at the gym, and goes home.  Since you're new, just about anything you do will get gains. That's where the majority of the weightlifting confusion and conflicting advice comes from. That, and there's more than a few "resources" out there looking to profit from your ignorance. Stick to a program of pullups, pushups, and bodyweight squats for a couple months and see where you're at. Feel free to bust your ass at it and don't be scared to have heavy days during the week with lots of volume. Your arms aren't going to turn green and fall off and the overtraining boogieman is largely a myth, so long as you eat and sleep enough. Mix and match what you do and try different shit like diamond pushups or uneven pullups when you get bored. If you have any more questions, feel free to PM. I've got some good weightlifting literature, if you're interested.

author: AlphaEnchantment
text_post: low reps are better for building muscle and strength and higher reps give you more of an aerobic workout. If your trying to cut down I would recommend going for a weight that you can get 8-10 reps. I would shoot for sets of 4-5 and finding a weight that you can hit atleast 8 reps without going to failure so you should feel like you have one or two more in the tank at 8 reps. This way when you dont go to failure your not as drained for the next set and you can get in more volume in your workout.  each week if you can try to increase your reps. so if you did 5 sets of 8 next time shoot for 5 sets of 9 or 10 and work your weigh up until you can get 12 reps then increase the weight. When you start losing weight and cutting your strength will also go down so try to lift as heavy as possible but when your not able to hit your numbers decrease the weight all in all whatever you do is going to work to some degree its just a matter of what works best

text_post: That sounds like a good plan. Lifting one day, then alternate jog or jump rope on the second is pretty solid.  I can recommend Ross Enamait's "Jump Rope Conditioning for Athletes". author: DBCooper
text_post: I love stiff legged/Romanian deadlifts with dumbells, the stretch/contraction is amazing. For squats with dumbbells try cleaning them into the front squat position - some guys like to hold them palms out, others, palms in: it depends on your bio mechanics and where your wrists feel most comfortable. Remember with dumbbell squats you're always going to be limited by how much you can clean, or how much you can hold in the farmer's-walk position if you're holding them to the side. Personally, I found holding them to the side was cumbersome. Really, a barbell would work much better - always. But as you explained when there's no access to a rack/barbells you can still get good work in.

The routine I have going is (in this order): 2 min jump rope 50 pushups  50 sit ups  50 jumping jacks 25 burpees Twice a day every day, once before I go to work, once immediately after I come home, weekends the same. Although it's a light workout, I've been doing this for three months, and the results have been pretty darn good so far, as in I definitely notice the change. However, I wonder about the balance. Any suggestions?

author: Teutatis
text_post: You need some pullups and some leg work in there. If you want to do a light workout every day I'd have at least 4 or 5 different days that I could rotate. There are a million different body weight exercises you can do, just look them up, create some kind of pull, push, legs routine. Have 4 or 5 different routines and just rotate between them. And then forget overtime to increase the number of reps, or sets or do the same amount of work in less time. But really, just move, that alone is good.

author: Anon-A-Moose
text_post: I did my workout routine technically yesterday.  Been doing it with minor variations for months. Sometimes I start with a few leg exercises, weighted lifts/leg press/leg curls/etc, occasionally add chest press.  Generally it revolves around bench with dumbbell curls for my rest period.  So bench/curl/bench/curl.  That's like 70+% of the workout there.  Then I switch to quarter squats (my lower back sucks), low rows, and hammer curls.  Occasionally I'll end with pullups and cable cross.  I need to find a really good chest isolation exercise to fit in, but in the meantime I burn more fat and get more done by putting complimentary exercises together and not taking much in the way of rest periods. I've noticed, I wanted to cut when I started this routine back in January.  I'm around 700 calories a day under maintenance.  Started at 175lbs and around 18% bodyfat.  Now I'm 175lbs and around 13% bodyfat.  Not sure how that works, but I like it.  My strength went up (5rm bench went from a low of 165 to 210ish, but my max bench from 260 to maybe 280, 300.  Curls went from 5x30lbs to 8x40lbs), and I'm visibly leaner--arms went from 16" to 15", but now have that "saran wrap" look, visible striations in shoulders when moving, etc.  So I'm not sure how my cut turned into recomp, but I like it.  Still, I need to switch up the routine more, and drop calories more too.  I hold fat poorly on my stomach due to loose skin.  Want to somehow hit 170 or even less by the end of the month.

author: WanderingSoul
text_post: 5/3/1 is supposed to be a great program.  It is best to go to it after you can no longer make strength gains per workout, or per week.  So start with something like Starting Strength or StrongLifts for 3-6 months (until you can no longer recover in time to keep making gains 3x per week).  Then jump to Madcow 5x5 or the Texas Method 5x5 where you make gains weekly.  Then after you can no longer make gains weekly, jump onto something like 5/3/1/ where you make gains roughly every month or so.  That's a good progression for someone looking to gain a lot of strength.  Obviously many different paths you could take, especially if you have different goals. My current plan is to finish out this 12 week cycle of Madcow, drop some bodyfat, and then slowbulk with something like this: http://www.jcdfitness.com/2009/01/lyle-m...g-routine/

author: dk902
text_post: I did 5/3/1 for around a year 1/2.  One cycle is 4 weeks which includes a reload week at the end. It's built around the big 4 lifts. The program is very simple and flexible, that's the great thing about it. It's for beginners and intermediates and can take you to a good level of strength.  Once you've been training for a while however you get to the point of diminishing returns. And you can't just dial in a program with linear progression and expect to make gains. So if you've been training for a long time, 5/3/1 is probably not for you.
